articles.title: A History of No Child Left Behind and the HISD Takeover
articles.author: Saron Regressa
articles.content: Where white and middle-class children are able to rely on cultural indicators to pass exams, minority and low-income students are subject to drills on the particular form of the test, multiple-choice questions, and specific writing skills that not only trade off with substantive learning, but actively “de-skills” students’ existing higher-order problem-solving and thinking. articles.title: AI’s Intrusion into Public Education
articles.author: Jake Colosa, Ann Finkel, Katie Punsly and Erin Tabor
articles.content: Think back to the first day of school when you were a kid. You walked into the building feeling nervous and excited to be reunited with friends, meet your teachers, and crack open your brand new supplies. Now imagine that instead of doing get-to-know-you activities with your classmates, you spend the majority of your day answering questions on a computer, and instead of your teacher picking out a book that she knows will spark your curiosity, you read AI-generated text on a screen. As students and teachers head back to school this fall, this is the bleak reality in more and more classrooms. Unless we fight back, the problem will only get worse. Tech oligarchs are seeking to colonize every part of our society, including public education, using tools like generative AI. Not only are students turning to AI, but districts and even unions are pushing teachers to incorporate AI into instruction. Some educators embrace it, arguing that we have to stay competitive so that students can get jobs upon graduation. They parrot the same arguments as tech CEOs, like Tim Cook of Apple who has said that workers need to use AI or get “ left behind.” Some educators worry that poor kids aren’t getting enough AI . Some claim that AI is here to stay, so we have the duty to teach students how to use it as a partner (The New York Times eagerly spotlighted a teacher who piloted an AI civics course). However, socialist teachers know better. We ardently believe that AI has no place in this human project of public education. Generative AI and the Encroaching Threat of Charter Schools Under capitalism, the profit motive is inescapable, even in public education. Education technology (edtech) is a $163 billion dollar industry , and an increasingly large share of that is dedicated to AI. Private interests like edtech companies and curriculum writers vie for multimillion-dollar contracts with public school districts. Districts themselves push to get more “value” out of each teacher by increasing class sizes and mandating scripted curriculums that de-professionalize educators and put money in the hands of corporations. An additional wrinkle with AI is data privacy. Districts need to ensure that teacher and student data is not being sold or used to train AI tools. These violations are not hypothetical; students and parents recently sued student surveillance software company Gaggle for violating constitutional rights. Miami-Dade schools paid $1.6 million to AI chatbot maker AllHere , which then filed for bankruptcy; its CEO was charged with fraud. This profit motive also opens the door to attacks from an evergreen enemy: charter schools. Charter schools, especially the private variety, have long claimed to provide the same education as public schools with less funding. In reality this is only possible by cutting corners and underpaying staff. It is common for charter schools to replace certified teachers with untrained individuals with euphemistic titles such as “guide” or “mentor.” Last year, an Arizona school board voted to allow online charter schools . One such school is Unbound Academy, which follows a 2 Hour Learning model: two hours of AI-administered academics a day and four hours of personal projects. The job posting for Unbound Academy guides shows a pay range from $40,000 – $60,000 a year with no benefits. Some of these jobs don’t even require a teaching license, will accept an expired license, or don’t require teaching experience. Such schools devalue the central importance of teachers’ expertise, acquired through years of training and experience. Listings boast that “associate guides” will be required to do zero content area teaching because it will all be done by AI. Instead, the guides’ role is to lead workshops on “life skills such as communication, creativity, problem-solving, and self-direction” and mentor students to “build confidence, ownership, and executive functioning.” Most of these articles are light on the details of what the actual day-to-day curriculum looks like. One state meets their requirement for its “English Learning” programming with Duolingo , an AI-powered app. These charter schools are not held to the same financial standards as an average public school. A San-Diego-based charter school spent $500,000 on two AI-powered humanoid robots that make factual errors, and alternately speak too quickly or too slowly for students. Meanwhile, Unbound Academy has budgeted $1000 per student on marketing, up to $350,000 per year for their program. This is unsurprising, as according to the National Center for the Study of Privatization in Education, charter schools spend more on administration and less on instruction per student than public schools. AI charter schools can also come with significant price tags. Charter school Arizona State University Preparatory Academy now offers Khan World School, a sixth to twelfth-grade online program where tuition can range from $8,250 to $13,700 annually, depending on where you live. Students are taught mostly asynchronously by “guides”. They have 24/7 access to Khanmigo, Khan Academy’s proprietary AI chatbot. There is a growing trend of replacing highly qualified teachers with underqualified guides, AI apps, and glorified search engines. The shift toward cheaper alternatives to human teachers has a negative impact on students in charter schools but also undercuts the ability of public school teachers to advocate for fair treatment and healthy classroom environments. Increasingly, even veteran teachers are feeling the temptation to be more like robots. AI as a “Time Saver” Many of our colleagues have used AI at work in varying ways to save time, and it’s hard to blame them: the average American teacher works 12 unpaid hours every week . But research shows that using AI at the workplace does not reduce workloads: it intensifies it through task expansion and increased multitasking. In an industry as scrutinized as public education, it is not hard to imagine what this might look like. Districts and school leaders already expect lengthy lesson plans and improvement directives. Excessive paperwork to justify our pedagogical decisions and improve meaningless test scores will only increase as AI adoption expands, further alienating teachers from our labor. Teachers should be skeptical when districts and tech companies claim to want to make our jobs easier and give us more control. From the assembly line replacing craftsmanship with mass production to surveillance software monitoring workers’ every move and click, the cost of technology-enabled increases in productivity is always borne by workers who are expected to produce more under increasingly alienated conditions. Similarly, we predict that not too far in the future, teachers will be required to do even more work during our precious few planning hours with the explicit mandate to use AI to supposedly manage the workload. We need to think carefully about our demands when it comes to AI in the workplace. The National Education Union , the largest education union in the United Kingdom, lays out clearly what they do not want as a result of their AI policies. They reject “the intensification of work for teachers” especially an increase of makework or busywork, “the loss of agency and autonomy,” the imposition of “pedagogical or curriculum approaches,” or a bandaid for “wider funding issues within our education system.” US teachers’ unions should adopt similar guardrails as we have conversations with our administrators around AI, set school-based and district-based policies, and fight for our union contracts. Unfortunately, we have not seen such vision coming from the leadership of our unions. The Need for Political Education and Action Rather than defending educators and students from this encroaching colonization, many of our own unions are welcoming the intruders. In 2025, the national AFT and the United Federation of Teachers in New York entered into a $23 million contract with Microsoft, Open AI and Anthropic. UFT President Michael Mulgrew claimed, “This initiative allows us to take control of AI in the education sphere and develop it for and by educators.” The initiative’s National Academy for AI Instruction tried to entice teachers by advertising less work and more efficiency. This message is Orwellian: “You’re not being controlled! You’re in control!” One year later, after pressure from rank-and-file, AFT President Randi Weingarten spoke with slightly more caution, admitting that “[r]esearch has established that less tech can produce better outcomes.” However, she maintained that AI “is here to stay,” so the best we can do is create a “balance” so that we can “harness the benefits of technology while mitigating the harms.” Against this current, some teachers are already successfully organizing against the imposition of AI on their work. Led by a caucus of rank-and-file educators, a coalition of parents and educators are calling for a two-year moratorium on the use of AI in NYC public schools. The coalition packed a panel in May, extending the meeting to seven hours while 100 parents and educators spoke against the city’s spending on student-facing AI. In September NYCPS announced a one-year moratorium on student-facing AI in 2-K through 8 classrooms . Similarly, the teachers’ reform caucus in Portland, Red Caucus, organized with parents over the last year to resist AI in schools.Their efforts successfully resulted in the school board unanimously voting to not renew any generative AI contracts. Our Role as Socialist Teachers We all remember a teacher who took the time to walk us through a lesson when we struggled, or performed a demonstration of a scientific principle that left us agog. As socialist teachers, we must call for public schools that create gardens which allow young people to grow in knowledge, wisdom, and creativity. A diploma from a public institution ought not be reduced to a declaration that you can “compete in the marketplace” but a celebration of your intellectual perseverance and wonder. Skilled human teachers, not robots, are unequivocally vital to creating such a garden. We can organize in our unions and alongside the families of our students to protect the classroom experience. Fighting for AI and data center moratoriums, protecting student and teacher data and privacy, and defending the integrity of our profession and communities are steps we can take in the immediate term as we organize for the long haul against the capitalist system that views schools as glorified jobs programs. To do so will take work, but it’s the kind of work that we have practiced day in and day out in the classroom: educating people and supporting them in taking on challenges. If we lead with our vision of human flourishing in public education, we can beat back the forces that seek to deskill our coworkers, our students and our society. articles.title: How a Canadian Union Finally Bested Walmart
articles.author: Benjamin Y. Fong
articles.content: In our hyperpolitical age , when mass protests come and go without much clear sense of what was won or lost, the strategies of social movements can seem quixotic, their benchmarks of success fuzzy. In the union world, however, success or failure can be measured in more cut-and-dried terms: by the ratification of a union contract. A contract between a union and an employer does not simply lay out the terms of employment at a particular worksite. It is also a symbol of the begrudging respect that an employer has for the collective organization of its employees. Until this year, Walmart had not put pen to paper on a union contract in Canada or the United States. As the largest employer in North America (with a headcount of 1.6 million in the US alone, it is still larger than Amazon) and with annual gross profits last year of $171 billion, Walmart has tremendous resources with which to fight off unions, and has developed a sophisticated playbook for doing so. It is not surprising that the company that labor historian Nelson Lichtenstein has called the “template organization” of neoliberal capitalism should have been, for most of its existence, an impenetrable anti-union fortress. This is why we should appreciate the weight of some recent news from Canada’s warehousing sector: on May 7, 2026, eight hundred workers at a Walmart Regional Distribution Center in Mississauga, Ontario (in the greater Toronto area), won a two-year contract after certifying their union with Unifor Local 252 in 2024. Though it has received relatively little coverage in the left-labor world, it is a truly historic victory, and a story that ought to be studied for its broader implications. No union gets a contract with a company as imposing as Walmart without there being lessons for organized labor to take from the strategy, tactics, and conditions that enabled the victory. The lumbering corporate retail giant that has for so long set the industry standard for working conditions has finally conceded to the union. Why now? Certification for Mississauga Before Unifor won in Mississauga in 2024, there had only been two prior union certifications — official government recognition that a group of workers is represented by a given union, creating a legal obligation to bargain — at Walmart facilities in Canada. One was at a store in Windsor, Ontario, in 1996 with the United Steelworkers, and it was only certified by labor board order in 1997 due to Walmart’s serious unfair labor practices during the election. The union never got a contract and was eventually decertified. The other was with the United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) in 2005 at a store in Jonquière, Quebec , which Walmart closed just after the union requested binding arbitration from Quebec’s minister of labor. As will become important in this story, Quebec, the neighboring province to Ontario, has strong enough labor law that certification there will almost always result in a contract. This is the dynamic that led Amazon to shutter its entire operation in the province last year. In the United States, the only successful election at a Walmart was in 2000, to unionize ten meat cutters at a Supercenter in Jacksonville, Texas. Days later, Walmart responded to what would otherwise have been minor news in rural East Texas by announcing that it was getting rid of all meat cutting in their Supercenters across the nation. In 2011, the UFCW attempted to organize the company as a whole with the multimillion dollar OUR Walmart campaign, organizing workers to engage in a wide variety of actions . Union elections, however, were not part of the mix, reflecting the recognition that the official path to unionization in the United States had been effectively blocked in cases where the employer was a corporation as well-resourced and with as much anti-union animus as Walmart. OUR Walmart had some notable wins, but the UFCW pulled funding from the campaign in 2015 when Marc Perrone assumed the presidency of the union. I am less familiar with Walmart’s arrangements with unions in Mexico, but it appears that many of the contracts that Walmart has signed there are so-called protection contracts , i.e., a collective bargaining agreement made without the workers’ knowledge or consent. By claiming to represent workers, those contracts, often signed by politically connected unions, “protect” the employer from any efforts by its employees to bargain more aggressively. Many such contracts were targeted by reforms promised by Andrés Manuel López Obrador­­ after he won the presidency in 2018. The next year, when the Revolutionary Confederation of Laborers and Farmworkers (CROC) planned a strike on a number of Walmart facilities, the company averted it with a 5.5 percent annual wage increase. But it is not clear that any new contract was signed between Walmart and CROC as a result of the settlement. So when Marty Gaouette, a worker in the shipping department at Walmart’s Mississauga Regional Distribution Center (RDC), reached out to Unifor Local 252 in December 2023 about the possibility of starting a union that would secure its gains through a legally binding contract, there was no real template in North America for doing so. But there were plenty of worker frustrations. At the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, Walmart had temporarily offered a wage bump (“hero pay,” the company called it, as part of the broader pattern of pandemic wage increases in the in-person retail sector) and flexible working hours. As unemployment numbers climbed, however, Walmart understood it had a relatively captive workforce and reversed course, eliminating the wage bump after just six months. “It was like the worst thing that they could have done to us,” explained Rhaddy Que, a utility associate in the maintenance department and eventually a member of the workplace’s bargaining team. “We were committed to work, but [they were] taking those dollars away from us.” Forced overtime was also a major issue. Unlike Amazon’s “mandatory extended time,” which is mostly enforced around holidays and Prime days, forced overtime became a year-round regularity in Mississauga, leaving workers with little control over their work-life balance. Speedup, in addition to longer hours, was increasingly an irritation. The Mississauga distribution center does what Walmart calls “store replenishment” — filling trucks destined for retail locations — and so has not traditionally been under the same management pressure as Amazon fulfillment centers, with their rapid delivery promises. But competitive pressure from Amazon has led Walmart to invest in its e-commerce capacity, offering last-mile delivery from its stores, and as it has done so, the need for greater and greater efficiency in replenishing inventory at Walmart stores has increased. Rodolfo “Tito” Pilozo, who was also on the Unifor bargaining team and works in receiving, says that the volume increase in the shipping department was what pushed Gaouette to contact the union. Management would say that they would have to process a certain number of cases of goods per hour, when in reality the amount was 10 percent more than announced. Speed-up, forced overtime, clawed back wages and benefits offered during Covid: these were swirling in the well of worker frustration in late 2023. The organizing work went quickly at first. A number of workers at the facility had been working there more or less since 1994, when Walmart first came to Canada. Back then, the warehouse had been located in Brampton, a neighboring auto manufacturing town also part of the greater Toronto area. It had been owned and operated by a third-party company, Tibbett and Britten, though those working there understood it was a warehouse for Walmart. Many of the workers who would lead the organizing in Mississauga had been previously involved with a unionization effort with the Teamsters at the facility in Brampton in the late 1990s. Tibbett and Britten moved the operation to Mississauga in 2002, according to Pilozo, and Walmart took full control of it in 2014. It was workers like Pilozo, with a great amount of seniority, who formed the core of the organizing team. Around April 2024, however, the organizing momentum slowed. Walmart’s captive audience meetings began to have an effect. “There was a lot of fear,” Que says about that moment. “They gave us that fear. We would have meetings, and they would just say how it’s not worth having a union. And that the company will do what the union is promising you.” Angela Drew Kimelman and Gary Rumboldt, the Unifor staff organizers assigned to the campaign, met with key worker organizers and they decided they were ready to make the campaign more visible. They formed “ Team Red ,” a group of workers who were willing to wear Unifor red to work on Wednesdays and who would leaflet outside the warehouse about the union. Unifor got so-called protection letters sent to Walmart on behalf of many of the organizing workers, which reminded the company that it was a violation of the rights of pro-union workers to be treated any differently than other workers. This gave Team Red the cover and confidence to organize publicly rather than in secret, as is often done in the early months of union drives. Justin Gniposky, Unifor’s organizing director, credits the strength of the team for patiently building strong connections during this time: We had a really strong inside committee. They spent the time, did the work. . . . Sometimes you don’t have that kind of structure on the inside, but these guys built that structure, they built it to succeed, and it showed. They had the respect of their co-workers, and respect’s one thing, but their co-workers also believed they had their best interests in mind. They had their trust to move through this. Part of building this trust lay in making sure that all union materials were translated into Punjabi, Tagalog, and Chinese. It also lay in getting workers who spoke these languages to reach out to other workers directly. This proved particularly important for getting the sizable part-time workforce on board with the union program. Most of the part-timers were international workers, some on temporary visas. Que estimated that even though at least 30–40 percent of those workers are no longer with Walmart, most of them supported the union when they were at the warehouse, despite many knowing they would not be around long enough to benefit from a contract. The Mississauga workers voted for their union from September 10 to September 12, 2024. Participation was high, and the union won with a reported 56 percent majority. Que expressed the disbelief that many felt about the victory: We weren’t sure at all [that we were going to win]. It was sort of embedded in our heads that Walmart is anti-union. You heard a lot that it was impossible to have a union, and that Walmart will not allow it. That’s what they made us feel. But later on, we started to feel like there was more power in people wanting to have the union than in Walmart not wanting one. Stemming the Tide The day after Ontario certified the union to represent the Mississauga warehouse workers, Walmart issued an across-the-board wage increase for every single logistics worker in Canada (warehouse workers and drivers both) — except for the eight hundred workers who had just unionized. As Gniposky summed it up, “Here’s the congratulations on getting a union. You are now making less than every single one of your coworkers.” Walmart also brought in workers from temp agencies to staff the Mississauga facility, signaling to the newly unionized workers that they could be easily replaced. Meanwhile, Unifor had other battles to fight with the company. In October 2024, the month after the election victory in Ontario, 120 Walmart truck drivers in British Columbia won card check certification. Soon after, 280 Walmart truck drivers in Alberta did the same. Peter Pearce, a driver out of the Nisku, Alberta, depot and member of the bargaining team there, said that it was “favoritism, nepotism, and unfair treatment by certain supervisors” that led the Alberta drivers to organize for union representation. To stem the tide of pro-union sentiment across the company’s Canada operations, Walmart issued yet another across-the-board wage increase. This made for two unprecedented countrywide wage increases in the span of a month and half, but the company made the message of these wage increases clear with the workplaces it excluded — the Mississauga RDC workers and the two units of truck drivers. Due to the particularities of Canadian labor law, the Mississauga warehouse workers’ and the western Canada truckers’ campaigns were run slightly differently. The warehouse workers petitioned for certification at the provincial level by the government of Ontario, while the drivers petitioned the federal government, as truck drivers crossing provincial or international borders are regulated federally. In Ontario, unions need 40 percent of workers to sign a union card before filing for an election, and a simple majority in an election to be certified. Federal elections are run by “card check,” meaning that a union need only get 50 percent plus one on cards to certify. Canadian labor law also has what is called a “ freeze provision ,” which prevents employers from altering workers’ terms and conditions during a certification drive, including by withholding standard wage increases. As the wage increases and other retaliatory actions by Walmart clearly violated the freeze provision, Unifor filed unfair labor practice (ULP) charges at both the provincial and federal levels. The Ontario labor board delayed the decision on the union’s charges until after collective bargaining ended, but the federal ULP was settled in November 2025. In the meantime, in May 2025, Walmart had sold off its Canada fleet service to a third party named Canada Cartage. This meant Unifor had to update its certification, which delayed negotiations, and Canada Cartage began a decertification drive. Pearce, the Alberta truck driver, described those negotiations as “extremely difficult.” The bargaining team pushed for a three-year contract, a 2.5 percent wage increase per year, and a limitation on “lease ops” subcontracting to no more than 10 percent of their work. Even though the federal labor board halted the decertification drive, as decertification is not allowed during active collective bargaining, Canada Cartage management did everything to slow things down. During the negotiations, the bargaining team got word that a sizable group of previously anti-union drivers in Calgary decided they now wanted the union to sign a sweetheart deal: a one-year contract, a 1.5 percent wage increase, and a lease ops limitation to 25 percent. “It made absolutely no sense,” Pearce said. “It scream[ed] of manipulation by management. ‘Please don’t give me extra money.’ I’ve never heard anybody say that.” The Unifor drivers eventually settled on a one-year collective agreement with Canada Cartage that expires in May 2027. But things ended quite differently for workers at the RDC across the country in Ontario. First Contract Collective bargaining in Mississauga finally started in May 2025, eight months after a majority of the warehouse’s workers voted for Unifor representation, and the same month Walmart sold off its Canadian trucking operations to Canada Cartage. As is often the case with intransigent employers, Walmart offered Unifor only a few sporadic dates over the subsequent months when it would be available for negotiations. With longer deadline rules for negotiations than there are in Quebec, Walmart intended to drag out the Ontario process as long as possible. Unifor’s bargaining team consisted of seven workers as well as Unifor’s national bargaining representative, Shayne Fields, and the longtime president of Local 252, Eamonn Clarke, who the year before had won a strike by four hundred workers at a plant owned by Nestlé. This team brought an intimidating amount of collective experience at Walmart. According to Pilozo, The good thing about our bargaining committee is that the people chosen were very senior people: twenty-nine, thirty, thirty-one, twenty-eight years with the company, and so on. When we first introduced each other, they [the Walmart negotiators] were very impressed. Their facial expressions showed that, “Wow, these guys have been there for a long time, almost since the beginning.” Even their lawyer was stunned. To negotiate, Walmart sent a delegation of nine company representatives. There was little indication that the company intended to bargain in good faith. According to a few of my interviewees, company management was actively supporting a decertification campaign, giving some anti-union workers special lockers in the building to hold decertification petitions and anti-union literature. Some workers who spoke out against the union got special treatment. Verbal altercations would break out, and at one point there was a physical fight between two employees, one pro- and the other anti-union, both of whom were suspended and later fired. According to Que, however, on the basis of Team Red’s inside connections, most workers understood these altercations to be a product of Walmart’s actions, not the union’s. I asked everyone I interviewed for this story if there was ever a moment where it felt like negotiations shifted, where Walmart seemed to turn a corner and begin to negotiate in good faith. That moment never seemed to come for anyone. It seemed more that, unlike in the United States, there was a limit on just how long the company could drag out negotiations because in Ontario, Unifor had the right to apply for an arbitrated settlement if collective bargaining ran aground. On May 7, 2026, a year after negotiations had officially begun, Walmart and Unifor announced they had reached an agreement. The resulting two-year contract was, by everyone’s account, not the “best” contract they could have gotten, but it was a meaningful one: wage parity with other warehouses; retroactive back pay for violating the freeze provision, in the form of a lump sum payment in the range of $4,000 to $9,000 per worker in July of this year; a “me too” clause preventing Walmart from raising wages elsewhere without raising wages in Mississauga, as they had done in the fall of 2024; planned wage raises in 2027 and 2028; a grievance procedure; and a limit on temporary workers. That last bit, according to Gniposky, got the biggest applause at the contract ratification meetings. The next day, Local 252’s Walmart members ratified the contract by a whopping 93 percent. Que and Pilozo told me that management is slowly acclimating to the new environment. Pilozo said he corrected a manager the other day who was complaining to workers about “your” contract: “It’s our contract, because it was signed collectively by the employer and us.” The manager apologized on the spot. Que said the new grievance procedure is working well, and that communication between stewards and management has improved to the point where they only invoke it occasionally. When I was interviewing them for this story, the lump sum payment was just days away, and workers were giving knowing nods to each other around the warehouse. In Pilozo’s words, where tension had existed not so long ago, “you’re starting to see smiles.” Location, Resources, Regulatory Constraint, Leadership “Workers at Walmart in the US and Canada have long made it clear that they want a union,” Nelson Lichtenstein told me. “To actually have a signed contract is a major breakthrough and something genuinely new when it comes to the largest private employer in North America.” Still, this story might seem a bit anticlimactic: big union wins are supposed to end in heroic confrontations before the company concedes. But no dramatic confrontation ensued here. Again, the billion dollar question is: Why was this the moment for Walmart to finally cave and sign a union contract? Are they getting soft in their old age, without Sam Walton’s infamous hatred of unions to guide the way? I would boil down the key factors in this historic victory to four: location, resources, regulatory constraint, and leadership. First, the fact that this happened in Mississauga was no accident. “Mississauga is a hub for most of Ontario and Quebec,” Gniposky explained. “That facility is important. It’s not as easy for them to move.” The company regularly warned workers that a pro-union vote could lead the facility to shut down, but the threat was a weak one. For one, the facility was an RDC and not a store (unlike the location in Jonquière, which Walmart shut down after they won union certification), and, in the Walmart supply chain, the RDC is in a key staging ground for two of Canada’s major metro markets, Toronto and Montreal. Walmart doesn’t have distribution centers in Quebec — having already closed them allegedy on account of the province’s strong labor law — but that market is easily supplied from Mississauga. Unlike the largest warehousing area in the United States, the sprawling Inland Empire in southern California, Canada’s primary warehousing cluster is nestled in a narrow corridor of the west Toronto suburbs. Stretching from Mississauga to Brampton, it is constrained on all sides: to the south by Lake Ontario, the east by Toronto, the west by suburban residential development, and the north by lack of infrastructure (and eventually Lake Huron). In other words, it would be a huge pain for Walmart to relocate this RDC. Distribution centers are already more strategic organizing targets than stores, on account of the disruptive impact that labor can theoretically cause through their organization. But distribution centers that can’t easily be moved are ideal targets. Choke point analysis — based on the idea that organized labor is going to be most successful at points in the production and distribution process where the disruptive impact of labor actions is relatively high — has a mixed reputation in the labor world. In part, this is because it involves the idea that some sites of work are more structurally important to a company’s operation than others, and thus that some workers’ struggles are more strategic or important than others. But when it comes to the contemporary logistical economy, in which the flow of commodities has increased in speed and efficiency but also fragility, and at a moment when labor is limited in the resources it can allocate to any organizing campaign, choke point analysis matters more than ever. Organized labor ignores it at its own peril. None of this is to say that Walmart will not attempt to move the RDC in Mississauga. Unifor and the RDC workers are well aware of this, which is why Pilozo, Que, and their fellow members of Team Red have been leafleting at other Walmart distribution centers all over the western suburbs of Toronto, aiming to saturate the area with union drives to give Walmart no geographic out. When Mississauga workers had been excluded from the prior wage bumps, their plight served as a cautionary tale for other Walmart workers, who benefited from disengagement. But now that the Mississauga workers have a hefty lump sum of back pay and contractually guaranteed raises set for 2027 and 2028, Unifor can persuasively make the case that the Team Red workers at Mississauga have been setting the standard for warehouse workers throughout the entire region. Second, this was not simply a scrappy, bottom-up drive. Unifor had invested serious resources into becoming Canada’s warehousing union. Gaouette reached out to Unifor because he had heard of the union’s Warehouse Workers Unite campaign, the fruit of its strategic analysis of the warehousing sector. Unifor was 100 percent committed to seeing the campaign through and leveraged the threat of arbitration, a costly and time-consuming process, as well as the combination of federal and provincial ULPs, to push the Mississauga campaign to the finish line. Note that the federal disclosure from the trucking negotiations hung over the provincial proceedings only because Unifor was willing to pursue Walmart on multiple fronts. This is the story of a committed group of trusted workplace leaders, but it is also one of a union with a long-term strategic vision and the will to back up that vision with resources. Third, Unifor strategically used the constraints of Canadian labor law to make it so that Walmart ultimately had nowhere to go. This is the big difference between the Canadian and American contexts: especially now, when most of the gains of the Biden-era National Labor Relations Board have been reversed, it’s difficult to imagine even a very skillful union in the United States using ULPs and the lingering possibility of arbitration to push toward a contract, as Unifor did in this case. This is not to say, however, that the question of regulatory constraint is not applicable, simply that it must be asked differently: in New York City, for instance, the Delivery Protection Act under consideration by the city council could upset Amazon’s delivery driver subcontracting model, providing the conditions for major wage gains and organizing drives. In many states, and many more municipalities, ballot initiatives can be used to put such regulatory questions governing employment relationships directly before voters. Looking longingly over the border at Canadian regulatory constraint should be cause not for lamentation, but for creative approaches to improving the odds of union drives in the United States. Finally, it’s overwhelmingly clear that the Mississauga RDC has a robust layer of trusted workplace leaders who not only bore an intimidating amount of collective work experience at Walmart and were committed to the union but also had the respect and trust of their colleagues to easily weather any storm that the company created. “Walmart saw that they weren’t going to be able to manipulate and turn these workers against each other,” Gniposky said. “Certainly there were anti-union people, as there are in any workplace, but they were a minority, and the majority was clearly on the side of their union. This was the strongest inside committee I’ve seen in my career.” It’s notable that there were no strikes, walkouts, or even marches on the boss in this story. As Que explained, “We educated all our members and said, ‘Maybe the best thing would be to have a strike.’ But we didn’t have to to get this collective agreement done.” If a strike was what was needed, Team Red was prepared to make it happen, and, by all accounts, it would have had high, if not total, participation. But they were reluctant to go down that road. Most stories of successful first contract fights will not be so free of confrontational workplace actions, but they will certainly feature workplace leaders focused more on the resolution than the conflict — people who want to work, to put in the work, and to proudly wear a union shirt while doing so. articles.title: Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings: Rape, Slavery and the Myth of Consent
articles.author: Robert Jensen
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Conclusive evidence is in from DNA tests : Thomas Jefferson fathered children with Sally Hemings. To put it more bluntly: The primary author of the Declaration of Independence and third president of the United States raped one of more than 600 people he enslaved, starting when she was a teenager. Does that seem disrespectful or ahistorical? First, let’s deal with the often-heard claim that we shouldn’t judge people of another era by the standards of our time. Jefferson’s defenders argue that, yes, he enslaved people and expressed ugly racist beliefs, but those practices and ideas were prevalent in the world in which he lived, implying there was no way he could have acted or thought differently. This approach avoids a simple question: Were there people expressing alternative ideas at the time? Jefferson’s Era Had Voices That Condemned Slavery Of course there were—not only people of African descent but also some of Jefferson’s peers. Among them was Thomas Paine, another major figure in the establishment of the United States who is best known for his 1776 pamphlet Common Sense . What is less well known about Paine is that he was an active opponent of slavery. The year after he arrived in America in 1774, he published an anti-slavery article in the Pennsylvania Journal and the Weekly Advertiser. A few weeks later an anti-slavery society was formed in Philadelphia, with Paine as a founding member. His article started with a clear condemnation of slavery and the Americans who supported it: That some desperate wretches should be willing to steal and enslave men by violence and murder for gain, is rather lamentable than strange. But that many civilized, nay, Christianized people should approve, and be concerned in the savage practice, is surprising; and still persist, though it has been so often proved contrary to the light of nature, to every principle of Justice and Humanity, and even good policy, by a succession of eminent men, and several late publications. Jefferson certainly was familiar with Paine and the arguments against slavery. Jefferson certainly was aware of the existence of the idea that all humans had an equal claim to liberty and the argument that Africans should be considered human in these matters. There were many different ideas about the institution of slavery and racism in play at the time. We‘re not judging Jefferson by the standards of our time when we point out how he used racism to justify the barbarism of slavery. We are acknowledging that others in Jefferson’s time—including the man who wrote “These are the times that try men's souls” in The American Crisis —articulated anti-slavery and anti-racist principles, at the same time Jefferson was in 1781 writing in his “Notes on the State of Virginia” about the natural inferiority of Black people. This essay is adapted from my 2005 book, The Heart of Whiteness: Confronting Race, Racism and White Privilege. Jefferson’s Own Writing Revealed His Racist Beliefs In that work, Jefferson explained that skin color is crucial, which led him to conclude, “Are not the fine mixtures of red and white, the expressions of every passion by greater or less suffusions of colour in the one, preferable to that eternal monotony, which reigns in the countenances, that immoveable veil of black which covers all the emotions of the other race?” Smell was an issue for Jefferson as well. Blacks “secrete less by the kidnies, and more by the glands of the skin, which gives them a very strong and disagreeable odour,” he explained. Among his other “insights” into Africans: --“They seem to require less sleep. A black, after hard labour through the day, will be induced by the slightest amusements to sit up till midnight, or later, though knowing he must be out with the first dawn of the morning.” --“They are at least as brave, and more adventuresome. But this may perhaps proceed from a want of forethought, which prevents their seeing a danger till it be present. When present, they do not go through it with more coolness or steadiness than the whites.” --“Comparing them by their faculties of memory, reason, and imagination, it appears to me, that in memory they are equal to the whites; in reason much inferior, as I think one could scarcely be found capable of tracing and comprehending the investigations of Euclid; and that in imagination they are dull, tasteless, and anomalous.” On the question of sexuality, Jefferson believed in the “superior beauty” of whites, noting “the preference of the Oranootan [orangutan] for the black women over those of his own species.” He also observed that black men “are more ardent after their female: but love seems with them to be more an eager desire, than a tender delicate mixture of sentiment and sensation.” It is unclear whether when Jefferson had sex with Hemings he was trying to provide a little tenderness in her life that Black partners apparently could not. Nor is it clear whether Jefferson spent much time wondering whether his preference for a Black woman meant he had something in common with the Oranootan. I don’t pretend to have insight into Jefferson’s state of mind or motivations. Sally Hemings Was Enslaved and Just 14 When She Went to Paris with Jefferson While it may seem harsh to many Americans, Jefferson raped Hemings, likely starting when she was 14 and he was 44. That description is not defamatory. Rape is defined as sex without consent. Slaves do not consent to their enslavement. To ask whether an enslaved person consents to any specific command from an enslaver is a meaningless question. Jefferson owned Hemings. Jefferson had sex with Hemings. Therefore, Jefferson raped Hemings, who under conditions of enslavement could not give meaningful consent. That conclusion doesn’t deny that Hemings and other enslaved people had some measure of agency, depending on their circumstances, and could make thoughtful choices. It only acknowledges legal and social facts. This is hardly surprising, given that white slave owners routinely raped their slaves. When stated generically—“white masters sometimes raped their African slaves”—the statement doesn’t spark controversy. What reason is there to assume Jefferson was different? Yes, he denounced slavery as immoral and politically untenable, but he continued to own other human beings so that he could live in the manner to which he had become accustomed. Why would we expect him to be incapable of forcing at least one of them to have sex? Why should the same term applied to other enslavers not be used to describe Jefferson’s conduct? How Romantic Language Sanitizes Sexual Violence Many Americans seem to need to tell a different story about Jefferson, even when acknowledging these realities. Take, for example, the way a liberal television journalist, the late Bill Moyers , described the interaction between master and slave as he discussed “the contradiction at the heart of the American experience”: The hands of Thomas Jefferson that wrote, “life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness,” also stroked the breasts and caressed the thighs of a slave woman named Sally Hemings, who bore him six children and whom he never acknowledged. It’s not clear how Moyers knew that Jefferson “stroked” and “caressed” Hemings, given that rapists typically do not concern themselves with the experience of their victims. It is possible Jefferson developed feelings for her that were manifested in some degree of tenderness and that the tenderness was reciprocated. Without evidence, it’s difficult to know. What we do know is that Moyers’ choice of language elides the reality of the relationship between enslaver and enslaved, turning rape into lovemaking. Some may want to dismiss all this as self-righteous moralizing or DEI propaganda. It’s neither. Following the facts is not the imposition of ideology but a step toward honest history, toward acknowledging that the stories that some prefer to tell about this country are as much myth as fact. Better to face the ugly, brutal, violent racist history of the country; understand that our affluent society is the product of that history; and then recognize that such violence continues to protect our affluence and perpetuate racialized disparities in the worldwide distribution of wealth. Why Honest History Must Confront Jefferson’s Contradictions It matters whether we tell the truth about what happened centuries ago, just as it matters whether we tell the truth about more recent history. If we can’t, we will never honestly face the present, which does not bode well for the future.

articles.title: Statement from UAW President Shawn Fain on Corporate Greed at GM
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content: This morning, GM announced the largest stock buyback in US automaker history. The company is planning to give another $20 billion in profits to Wall Street while tens of thousands of autoworkers have no retirement security, while plants sit under-utilized, and while the global auto industry overtakes GM. This company has spent $30 billion on stock buybacks and dividends in the past 5 years alone, while kicking and screaming about costs during our 2023 negotiations. We will remember when we are back at the bargaining table in 2028. Let’s be clear about what stock buybacks really are. They are a form of legalized mass looting, sending billions of dollars generated by the working class directly to Wall Street investors who’ve never seen the inside of a factory. Why don’t 80 percent of GM’s autoworkers have a pension and retirement healthcare, as they did for half a century? Because someone on Wall Street is collecting their pension check in the form of a goddamn stock buyback. Why is GM nickel and diming their retirees while lavishing shareholders with billions? Because this company has sold its soul to Wall Street. Who benefits? The majority of stocks in this country are held by the wealthiest one percent. Who’s the largest individual shareholder at GM? CEO Mary Barra, who made $48 million in 2025, a 60 percent raise in a year. And just five Wall Street firms — companies like Blackrock and State Street — will get nearly $7 billion out of this scam. Corporate America is destroying this country by looting the rust belt to pay off millionaires and billionaires for short term gain, while our factories sit empty and our working class falls further behind. GM hasn’t built a new plant in this country in 20 years. When GM is spending $20 billion buying back their own stock but only half that investing in factories, equipment, and productive capacity, they are choosing Wall Street profits over blue collar America . When we bargained our UAW contract with GM in 2023, the media and the company acted like it was the end of the world for autoworkers to get a raise. But there’s always tens of billions of dollars for Wall Street. So when we return to the bargaining table with GM in 2028, I want the American public, the American politicians, and the American autoworker to remember this day. If there’s $20 billion for Wall Street, you better believe there’s our fair share for the working class.

articles.title: Even Musk Haters Will Hate Sitting Through Musk
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: Always glad to see Elon Musk pummeled, of course, as he is in Alex Gibney’s documentary Musk , now playing in theaters. The film sounds the alarm over this right-wing trillionaire tech bastard, which can’t be done too early or too often. But there’s a problem when even I, a fervent, long-term Musk hater, get exhausted, then irritated, then fed up by this film long before its grueling four-hour running time is over. For me, the burning question quickly became: Who is this film for? What’s the intended audience for this thing? Gibney’s huge, heavy-handed disemboweling of Musk, clumsily wielding an axe rather than a scalpel, was immediately identified as “a hit piece that misses, and makes the fatal sin of being boring for 4 hours” by Musk himself , warning off his obsessed fans, who’ll obviously be skipping the film. It’s an indication of Musk’s essential stupidity — his cluelessness about everything except how to generate profits, particularly off his own repeated business failures — that he keeps obsessively commenting on this film on social media, thus doing its publicity work for the PR team presumably getting paid to do the same job. Some curiosity-seekers with time to kill might head to the multiplex, thanks to the many free, self-defeating, Elon Musk–generated promo tweets. The obvious audience for the film would seem to be the many who despise Musk. That’s a vast number of sane people: political leftists; the legions screwed over by him in business deals or working for him in thankless, underpaid jobs; those fired by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and those infuriated by the firings; the hapless car enthusiasts suckered into driving malfunctioning Teslas; and anyone who keeps up at all with Musk’s role in the latest sinister predations of the high-tech industry in league with right-wing governments around the world. But consider that these are the people in the know, already aware of Musk’s harrowing South African childhood, early business failures that nevertheless made him huge profits, insidious credit-stealing takeover of the Tesla car company, SpaceX ventures, self-driving car and Twitter/X and DOGE debacles, appalling personal life, including the fathering of at least fourteen children by many different women in order to spread Musk seed around the world, and all the rest of it. These potential spectators are perhaps the least likely to feel the need to torture themselves with even more intimate knowledge of a man famous for the widespread repugnance inspired by his ideas, his rhetoric, his practices, and his bizarre physical self-presentation. I personally feel I deserve a medal for having sat through Musk . Or at least a care package full of soothing home-spa products from a concerned citizens group. Who Is This Four-Hour Takedown For? That leaves, as potential audience members, those who don’t know much about Elon Musk or are totally indifferent to him. And obviously those lucky, oblivious citizens aren’t going to create a rush of ticket-buying either. Oh, and one other tiny group of possible Musk -watchers includes cinephiles who are always interested in what’s being done in the documentary form. They’re all flocking to see the other documentary that opened last week, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything , a total wow of a film that’s drawing in crowds far beyond the size of the usual audience for documentaries. It took in about $15 million its first weekend; Musk made about $315,000 on more than four hundred screens. But if some of those spectators go above and beyond the call of cinephile duty and watch Musk too, they’ll be depressed at best, and appalled at worst. It’s a sloppy job, Musk , reflecting a juvenile sensibility. It’s constantly presenting slapdash footage and recorded voices that aren’t identified or attributed to any source, and it’s loaded with what I guess must be Alex Gibney’s idea of infotainment stylings intended to make documentaries popular with the masses. Because Musk wouldn’t sit for an interview, for example, Gibney mined his interviews with other filmmakers and journalists and podcasters to digitally generate an AI avatar of Elon Musk who speaks as he might speak if he could be persuaded to speak to the filmmaker. This is clearly Gibney’s idea of a big “gotcha” triumph, cleverly turning Musk’s massive AI investment against him. But really all it accomplishes is more misery for the half-dozen spectators in the theater, getting forcibly returned over and over to the bizarrely big-headed Musk avatar, made unaccountably handsomer than the actual golem-like real-life Musk, tricked out in leathers and enthroned in a gaming chair to deliver further inane commentary, such as musings on the possibility that we’re living in a simulation or that humans might turn out to be nothing more than “the biological bootloader” for digital superintelligence. The Pew-Pew-Pew Gamer Style In general, Alex Gibney seems to have made an attempt at form-follows-function in creating a documentary that’s extremely Musk-like, resulting in an overall sense of slovenly gigantism that’s nevertheless unimpressive: a film as crude, outsize, erratic, and shambling as the man himself. For example, Gibney resorts to endless comic book and video game effects, favorite Musk pastimes, in order to present Musk’s rampage through the world. The first time we see a lengthy sequence involving first-person-shooter-style animation to represent Musk’s takeover of Twitter, blasting thousands of employees who actually know how the business runs, mass firings that help Musk turn a sometimes profitable company into a free-falling flop called X, it’s barely endurable. But then we have to watch the same extensive pew-pew-pew gamer massacres a second time, now with Musk’s notorious chainsaw repurposed as a firing weapon, to represent DOGE’s rampage through various US government buildings. It stands for the firing of legions of highly competent officials early in Donald Trump’s second term, before Musk had a spat with Trump and DOGE was shut down. By this point, it’s merely infuriating on too many levels to count. Doomerism in Place of Politics The message of Musk , just to save you the trouble of actually sitting through the film, especially if you’re a leftist thinking that you really ought to go see it, is that it’s hopeless to resist Elon Musk’s fascist takeover. It’s already too late. Musk has amassed so much wealth, accrued so much political influence among the worst of the worst of global leaders, and created such extensive surveillance systems worldwide, the only thing to do is wait for him to officially declare himself as a comic-book supervillain come to life, having finally achieved world dominance, and probably called something stupid like GreatX, Overlord of the Galaxy. And the attitude Gibney adopts — gloating over our guaranteed collective doom — serves the lunatic right, the fascist Musk-lovers of the world, very well. Why bother organizing when we’re all going to die? Musk starts and ends with the sublime imagery of outer space, which is promptly despoiled by Elon Musk and his imagined colonization of all of it (“I want to die on Mars,” he once mused), which began with SpaceX, represented in Musk as his most successful company in spite of all those crashing rockets. If the film succeeds in its mission to induce widespread cynical despair, you’ll be thinking the human race needs to end if only to prevent Musk from getting his big dumb mitts on other planets after he destroys the earth. articles.title: Socialize All Housing
articles.author: Mike Beggs
articles.content: In 1872, the German socialist newspaper Der Volksstaat ran a series of articles on housing. The breakneck growth of industrial cities had brought overcrowding, squalor, and soaring rents for workers. Their author, Arthur Mülberger, drawing on the ideas of the French anarchist Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, offered a simple solution — tenants should become owners. In the scheme, rental payments would be transformed into something like a mortgage payment. Eventually, every worker would hold the title to their own home. Friedrich Engels was unimpressed. In a series of replies later collected as The Housing Question , the cofounder of Marxism dismissed Mülberger’s plan as both impractical and political malpractice. Elsewhere in the same work, criticizing the reformer Emil Sax, he warned: “Give them their own houses, chain them once again to the soil and you break their power of resistance to the wage cutting of the factory owners.” For Engels, the answers to the housing question would only be made possible through the abolition of the capitalist mode of production. A century and a half later, the Left is still battling over housing. In a certain populist sense, Mülberger won the argument with Engels. Across the world, homeownership has become a defining ambition of working-class life, and the housing crisis is often framed as a crisis of access to it. Meanwhile, much of the debate on the Left today is framed as a fight between YIMBYs and NIMBYs. One divide is between those who seek to impede market-rate construction, arguing that it can fuel displacement and offers too little to low-income renters, and those who support construction with fewer caveats to boost supply and the bargaining power of renters along with it. We can all agree on building social housing, but so far that hasn’t materialized into a program on the scale of the crisis. However, it’s worth stepping back from these fights and asking what ultimate vision we are fighting for. In what follows, we set aside the thorny problems of transition — how we get from here to there and who will fight for it — and sketch out a maximalist vision of socialist housing. Our answer builds on Engels’s critique of Mülberger while putting aside his reluctance to offer details about the possible shape of a socialist future. We advocate the abolition of private ownership of housing and a fully socialized housing system. A Blueprint for Socialized Housing A home of your own — one you can shape to your tastes and needs, and that you feel secure in — is a genuine good worth preserving. But capitalist homeownership binds together choices about your home with choices about finance and wealth that inevitably come with risks, and the dynamics of the housing market are prone to generate arbitrary inequalities. In a socialist economy, we could preserve that security and freedom while socializing the financial risks and gains of housing. Engels warned that “to speculate as to how a future society would organize the distribution of food and dwellings leads directly to utopia.” But given the “capitalist realism” we seem stuck in today, we think the effort is worth it. In a capitalist society, housing inequality is more than a symptom of broader income and wealth inequality. Homes are both places to live in and vehicles of wealth. In fact, owner-occupied housing alone accounts for about half of gross household wealth in most of the twenty-nine Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries covered in a 2022 study . Individuals often hold business wealth through shares, investment funds, and pensions, but they tend to own dwellings directly, whether they live in them or rent them to others as a landlord. Housing wealth is very unevenly distributed, but owning a home is a widespread experience and ambition, and the fact that it is such a personal form of wealth for owner-occupiers complicates the politics of inequality in contemporary capitalism. Housing makes up most middle-class assets in most OECD countries, and accumulating that wealth is often a lifetime project involving paying off a mortgage over many years. Many of the features that make housing unusual as a consumer need would persist under socialism, so it calls for special consideration. Housing stock is expensive to produce and very long-lasting if maintained. It occupies space in particular locations. People care about where they live — in terms both of their home’s position relative to other places that matter to them and of the character of the natural and built environment around it. There is an ineradicable element of scarcity to desirable locations. A given patch of land can be used more or less densely, modifying the supply of dwellings in an area, but density and type of housing are themselves aspects of a location that people care about. Households deciding whether to meet their housing needs by renting or by taking out a mortgage can compare expected interest, maintenance, tax, and insurance costs, along with transaction costs and the opportunity cost of the money tied up in the home, with the rent on an equivalent property. Some households may be willing to pay a premium for the security of ownership and the freedom of renovating; on the other hand, the illiquidity and risks of ownership may lead others to prefer to rent. For some, there is no choice: since mortgage borrowing generally requires a deposit and the lender’s confidence in the borrower’s ability to repay, many of those on low or insecure incomes are unable to finance a purchase. Then there are capital gains. Even gains driven by rising incomes and population can be arbitrary — windfalls unrelated to anything the homeowner has done. Such gains can widen a wealth gap between homeowners (and their descendants) who got in early and those stuck renting or only “getting on the property ladder” later in life. There are a number of ways a socialist society might structure the provision of housing. We suggest a simple approach. In our model, the land and housing stock are publicly owned, but households have secure tenure in the dwelling they live in and the capacity to renovate to their taste. People make regular rental payments for housing, rather than being involved in a financial relationship paying off a large asset purchase over decades. Households take neither the property-price risks nor the capital gains that come with ownership — these are socialized — while the system aims to preserve the security and freedom of a place to call their own. Rents are set by a housing authority, generally aiming to match demand to supply. A household’s rent may shift over time according to changes in supply and demand for dwellings that are similar in location and type. In other words, rents adjust in response to market conditions and are not simply set forever at the beginning of tenure, though movements can be smoothed to avoid sudden shifts. The housing authority is tasked with developing supply in response to projected demand, so that significant general increases in rent would be considered a policy failure to be remedied. Urban planning and development are in public hands and engage worker-managed construction firms to do the building. This system aims to allow each household to make its own housing choices, each bearing the appropriate cost, within a wider system of guaranteed minimum incomes and needs-based transfers that support those who could not otherwise afford adequate housing. Some may prefer a modest apartment so as to have more to spend on other things, while others put more of their budget into spacious villas. Many people will make different choices at different stages of life. The system can accommodate experiments in self-managed collective living for those who want it — as well as handling the traditional family home. Residents are custodians rather than full owners of their homes, but they can use and adapt them to their needs within agreed rules. They can initiate renovations in partnership with the housing authority or its associated bank. Instead of paying up front, the costs of renovations are factored into rents and paid over time. Because maintenance costs and depreciation are already baked into the rent of all dwellings, each comes with a budget and schedule for renovations. Households only need to pay extra for modifications that are idiosyncratic or costlier than the standard. The housing authority could adjust the pace of renovation to help smooth activity for the construction sector, which is notoriously cyclical in capitalism. If a lot of new construction is going on, renovation can be made temporarily more expensive or limited with a waiting list. When new construction slows, this can be reversed. The pace of renovation can also potentially be varied to help with macroeconomic stabilization beyond the sector. Because capitalist housing markets are riddled with externalities, housing is an excellent place to reduce the role of markets and open up a considerable role for public planning. Our model of socialist housing aims to accommodate the diversity of household preferences and needs and preserve the central features of “a home of one’s own” — without the individual property-price risks and windfalls that come with the capitalist model of ownership. A century and a half after Engels, that remains the answer to the housing question.
