articles.title: Trump’s War on Palestine Comes for Fergie Chambers
articles.author: Chip Gibbons
articles.content: On Tuesday, September 22, the Spanish Council of Ministers refused to block a US extradition request for James “Fergie” Chambers, a prominent and wealthy leftist activist and donor. The council did not determine whether the US citizen and activist will be sent to the United States, but only whether the request would proceed in Spanish courts, who will then make the final determination. Chambers’s legal team, which includes a number of legendary human rights lawyers, have vowed they will argue before the courts that Chambers’s extradition is politically motivated; thus granting it would violate the US-Spanish extradition treaty. The US indictment against the activist remains sealed, but Chambers’s lawyers have accused the US government of seeking to criminalize humanitarian aid to the Palestinian people, which has been a priority for Chambers to provide. The US extradition request has aroused considerable controversy within Spain. The electoral platform Sumar, a junior partner in Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist-led government, has opposed the extradition, as have a number of Spanish parliamentarians. They not only view the move as at odds with current Spanish government’s support for Palestine but as aiding the Trump administration as it seeks to internationalize its repression of pro-Palestinian voices. The attacks on Chambers come at a pivotal time. For the last three years, as Israel has waged a genocidal war of annihilation in Gaza, Western governments have sought to shield the apartheid state from accountability by restricting their own citizens’ free speech rights. The United States has not been immune from this. It has escalated a long-standing trend of using its anti-terrorism laws and sanctions to target global support for the Palestinian cause. After inheriting this assault on free speech, the Trump administration has sought to broaden its scope across the Left. And as the State Department has repeatedly made clear, this program is not to be limited to the United States domestically. It is in this context that the extradition request for Chambers must be understood. A Witch Hunt Chambers is a self-described communist. He also is a former heir to the Cox cable family fortune. He divested from his family’s fortune, granting him $250 million. With this money, Chambers began funding left-wing groups. The multimillionaire garnered media attention, some of it highly inflammatory, over his role in supporting the Stop Cop City protesters, an Atlanta-based activist movement opposed to the building of the Atlanta Public Safety Training Center on a mix of environmental and anti–police militarization grounds. The movement itself has faced heavy repression, with the state of Georgia bringing widely condemned charges against sixty-one supporters of the movement. According to Chambers, he donated a “couple of million dollars” to groups opposing the facility, as well as hundreds of thousands in bail support for those arrested. Chambers also funded the defense of a group of activists who vandalized Elbit Systems offices in New Hampshire, part of an international movement of direct actions against the Israeli weapons manufacturer. Chambers’s funding of activist causes and his underlying radical politics did not go unnoticed by the US media. In 2023, Los Angeles Magazine ran an exclusive on Chambers under the headline “Heir to Cox Family Fortune: ‘I Chant Death to America Every Day.’” In 2024, Mother Jones ran a profile of Chambers’s support for Stop Cop City with the headline, “There’s a Communist Multimillionaire Fomenting Revolution in Atlanta.” Days later, Rolling Stone published its own piece, “Fergie Chambers Is Heir to One of America’s Richest Families — and Determined to See the U.S. Fall.” Since Chambers’s arrest, Mother Jones has again written about him under the headline “Meet the Multi-Millionaire Pro-Hamas Activist Who Was Arrested in Spain.” (Shortly after October 7, 2023, Chambers tweeted “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’. There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for. No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done anything wrong. It’s simply genocide. Like it has been.”) The fact that an heir to one of the largest fortunes in the United States is now funding very left-wing activism is certainly newsworthy. And while many of these headlines were clearly designed to draw readership, it does not appear these profiles misrepresented Chambers’s views or misquoted him. But the attention to Chambers came at a time when the Right was increasingly targeting those who funded left-wing protest movements. As part of these efforts to stamp out political movements they disfavor, the Right has once again turned to an old rhetorical playbook, claiming such protests are not organic expressions of dissent but the sinister machinations of outside forces. While in the past the Communist Party has played the role of boogeyman, and today the nebulous “antifa” frequently also plays that role, significant focus has been placed on the role of funders as the supposed puppet masters inciting unrest in the United States. Attacking such funders is a clear strategy in Donald Trump’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-7 (NSPM-7). Rhetorically, much of this attention has been devoted to the liberal, well-connected philanthropist, George Soros, and his son, Alex Soros. But in terms of the actual mechanics of repression, the targets have increasingly been individuals like Chambers, whose views are more outside the mainstream. On Capitol Hill, Republicans, egged on by right-wing media, have engaged in a witch hunt reminiscent of the McCarthy era against Neville Roy Singham, even going as far as to subpoena a news outlet that received funding from him. Singham has been a left-wing activist for decades. A former member of the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, Singham started his own software company, which he sold in 2017 for $785 million. Singham is the husband of Code Pink founder Jodie Evans, and his philanthropy came under fire as part of a series of attempts to demonize the venerable antiwar group as agents of China. Singham currently resides in Shanghai, and critics have asserted without evidence that he is an unregistered agent of China in order to taint the activism he funds. Anyone familiar with the McCarthyite campaign against him will immediately note that parts of NSPM-7 clearly allude to him. Fox News has played a significant role in fearmongering about Singham, so it is significant that in an article on Chambers’s arrest, the conservative outlet directly compared the two. In line with the Right’s growing narrative about US protests, the same article described Chambers as “bankrolling anti-cop, pro-Hamas communist revolution” and “years of financing anti-Israel and anti-West organizations and protests.” And while Chambers is certainly wealthy, unlike the Soroses, who fund mainstream causes and are close with powerful Democratic politicians, Chambers is certainly marginalized within US political life. With both Chambers and Singham, a huge factor in the attacks on them are their support for the Palestinian cause. It is this support that has now directly placed Chambers in the crosshairs of the Trump Justice Department. Human Rights Advocacy Is Too Much for Trump The US indictment against Chambers remains sealed, thus making it impossible to independently assess what the government is even alleging. According to his legal team and multiple media accounts, the indictment alleges money laundering in support of Hamas and “conspiracy to commit disorderly conduct.” The Grayzone , an independent media outlet focusing on US empire, claims to have viewed the sealed indictment. It describes the indictment as alleging “international money laundering. . . . with the intent to provide material support to and resources to foreign terrorist organizations.” In 2023, Chambers moved to Tunisia, though he has since relocated to Ireland. The indictment focuses on wire transfers Chambers made from banks in his native United States to banks in his then–home country of Tunisia. According to The Grayzone ’s Kit Klarenberg, while the indictment focuses on these transfers, the indictment offers no evidence Chambers gave money to any foreign terrorist organizations. Chambers’s partner, Stella Schnabel, has publicly claimed the money was transferred as part of Chambers’s backing of Club Africain, a Tunisian soccer team, and youth soccer programs in the country. Chambers also has donated money to the Sameer Project, a humanitarian charity in Gaza. According to Middle East Eye , Chambers’s donation “helped establish a bakery in northern Gaza, complete a desalination plant and operate a free medical clinic.” Since Chambers’s arrest, Sameer has not paused its vitally needed humanitarian work. Without having access to the indictment, or understanding the wider US government case, it is unclear what role this laudable humanitarian work plays in the United States’ case against Chambers. His lawyers and supporters have repeatedly brought it up in the context of the extradition. And the United States has a long history of criminalizing such humanitarian efforts, oftentimes working in tandem with Israeli intelligence to do so. In one of the signature prosecutions of the post-9/11 war on terror, the US government put five leaders of the Holy Land Foundation for Relief and Development on trial. They were not accused of supporting the 9/11 attacks, al-Qaeda, or even any act of violence. Instead, the Bush administration argued that the bona fide humanitarian aid they had sent to the occupied Palestinian Territories had gone through Hamas-controlled social-welfare committees, something the charity disputed. After two trials, and with help from the recently passed Patriot Act and Israeli intelligence services, they were convicted. The prosecution made clear that even pure humanitarian aid can be dubbed support for terrorism by the US government. Since Israel launched its genocidal war in Gaza, both the Biden and Trump administrations have escalated the use of this counterterrorism framework against Palestinian human rights advocacy. The Biden administration slapped Samidoun, a Palestinian prisoners’ rights group, with counterterrorism sanctions accusing them of being a sham charity. The Trump administration has continued this trend, including by sanctioning the organizers of the Freedom Flotilla on spurious claims that they are “terrorists.” It has also escalated by now sanctioning human rights groups and officials not accused of terrorism but of helping the International Criminal Court in attempting to prosecute Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. False allegations of terrorism are no longer necessary; mere human rights advocacy is enough. Such sanctions have sweeping reach, as the US government considers coordinating advocacy with a sanctioned party a violation of the sanctions regime, meaning US citizens seeking to work with these human rights groups or international officials risk prison sentences under the International Emergency Economics Powers Act by doing so. The Trump administration is also seeking the extradition of a Turkish national from the UK on claims that the charity he collected humanitarian aid for Gaza through was a “sham charity” on behalf of Hamas. In their press release announcing the request, the US Department of Justice explicitly thanked Israel’s domestic security service for their aid in the matter. And, in addition to internationalizing its attacks on aid for Palestine, it is also internationalizing its attacks on the Left. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Stephen Miller hosted a bizarre international conference on left-wing terrorism and are now extending the mania for sanctions beyond Palestinian human rights advocates to what it dubs “far-left terrorism.” This includes counterterrorism sanctions placed on Autistici/Inventati, an Italian volunteer collective that provides encrypted email services to activists. According to the Trump administration, they provided these services to “Marxist, anarchist, and other left-wing extremist groups in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere.” A Dark Precedent on the Horizon The United States’ extradition request has rightfully generated opposition. Sumar, whose members include the vice prime minister and labor minister, have opposed it, as have a number of leftist members of the Spanish parliament. Over 150 prominent international activists, including Greta Thunberg, signed a petition opposing it. In Spain, Chambers is represented by Baltasar Garzón, a prominent human rights lawyer who, as a judge, issued an arrest warrant for former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet. The Left in the United States should also rise to the occasion and demand their government drop this extradition. Chambers has certainly been a polarizing figure on the US left, to put it mildly. Many on the Left disagree with many of his views, and Chambers has not been shy about voicing his own criticisms of the US left. But faced with political repression from a Trump administration hoping to both stamp out the Left and willing to aid Israel’s genocide in Gaza, such internal differences of opinion do not matter. The situation is urgent to stand against political repression, not just for Gaza but the entire international left. If the Trump administration succeeds in getting their hands on Chambers, it will set a dark precedent. articles.title: Failing, Flailing, and Falling
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Imagine this: a completely blank page confronting me in the age of Donald Trump. What in the world can I say, given you know (exactly) whom? Who else could fill it but you know (exactly) whom (and the “m” on that “who” is, of course, for our very own “monster” president). Well, let me start with this: If I went back in time and tried to tell my parents or anyone else in that ancient world of my childhood and youth about a future Donald Trump presidency (and managed to explain–no small thing, believe me–who he would be and what he would do), there’s no question that I would have been laughed out of the room. I would have been considered a raving lunatic. I’m talking, of course, about the president who started a war with Iran over nuclear weapons that country doesn’t have and only recently said , “They [the Iranians] can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon. It’s essentially almost over with.” Buy the Book When it comes to those two California cities that voted for a Democrat for president last time around instead of You Know Exactly Who(m), well, sayonara . A very small price to pay indeed! And that’s “our” president making himself as plain as day–or do I mean as plain as night? Once upon a time, such language from an American president would have been considered the most ludicrous version of science fiction imaginable. And yet here we are not in the future but in this very moment, the second time around, and there he is–and you know exactly who(m) I mean–suggesting that the Iranians might “take out” a major West Coast city or two and he wouldn’t weep a single tear. (Oh, and only recently Secretary of Defense [no, War!] Pete Hegseth withdrew American B-1 bombers from a base in England–yes, England!–for fear of an Iranian attack, a distinct retreat of the first order.) And here I still am at 82 years old, living in a moment that, once upon a time, would have been considered beyond unimaginable, and I’m not even thinking of AI. Honestly, after all these years, I can hardly believe it! (And please, don’t even ask me what “it” is!) To tell you the truth, in fact–and I swear that it is the truth and nothing but the truth–there’s just so much I don’t believe about this ever-stranger world of ours. You know, the very one we’re all living in. As I was writing this piece, for instance, the U.S. military just blew to smithereens the 72nd (supposedly drug-running) boat that it’s annihilated in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean since September 2025, and that includes the most recent of the (and it’s probably an undercount) 239 people killed –until, that is, the Trump crew destroys yet more such vessels (as they undoubtedly will, possibly even before this piece comes out). Admittedly, it could be worse. Donald Trump has yet to decide to shoot down airplanes or blow trains off their tracks, or blast cars off some suspicious highway, but don’t count on any of those not happening either, not in this ever-stranger world of ours. What Goes Up Must Come Down Of course, once upon a (distant) time, we never could have imagined any of this, not in a million years. Oh, wait! Let me offer one exception to that. There is, in fact, something in the Donald’s world that any of us would have recognized back then. I’m thinking of his recent TV campaign ad swearing that “America will never be a communist country.” Yes, once upon a time in another universe, American politicians– Senator Joe McCarthy being the epitome of them–were indeed focused on commies (as they used to say) in a way that bore no relation to any reality in this country. Of course, back then, it still would have been inconceivable for an American president to spend your taxpayer dollars to put his own “anti-communist” (and, of course, wildly pro-Trump) campaign ads on television; no less, as the New York Times reported, personally instructing “his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency, setting in motion a $20 million contract that used funds from the Department of Homeland Security, according to people familiar with the matter.” Related: We're Up Shit's Creek Without a Paddle—and Trump Is Steering And yes, once upon a time, that would have been shocking even in the United States of America. But that, of course, was another universe. Today, in this strange, artificially unintelligent world of ours, it’s just a passing story and no big deal at all. Of course, like me, Donald Trump grew up in a world where there was supposedly no greater danger than “the commies.” At that moment in the 1950s and early 1960s, that also meant the other superpower of that (long-gone) era, the Soviet Union. (China, although already a communist country, had yet to rise to superpower status or even, in its own fashion, to be fully noticed here until Secretary of State Henry Kissinger paid a surprise visit to it in 1971 and then, in 1972, President Richard Nixon traveled there himself and met communist leader Mao Zedong in person.) Now, the latest Communist leader of that country, Xi Jinping, has flown directly to Washington, D.C. to put up with our all-too-mad president, while undoubtedly thanking the gods above that Donald Trump considers climate change a “ con job “ and has left green power and the future (such as it may be) to the rising imperial power on planet Earth. In fact, while Trump has taken control of our tax dollars to create self-glorifying ads for the Trump brand of government, China has made the production of green energy it’s imperial brand (even as it also pours fossil fuels into the atmosphere in an unparalleled fashion) Of course, all great powers rise and then (to repeat myself) fall in one fashion or another. Imperial decline is a given, even a distinctly repetitive part of human history. But there is certainly something new in Donald Trump’s version of falling or do I simply mean failing? In fact, I think I might add another “l” to that, too. He’s not just ensuring that imperial decline on this planet at this moment will be a failing but also a flailing operation (though, of course, you wouldn’t know it from him). After all, he’s quite literally turning over the future without anything in return to a rising China, leaving it alone to exploit a new kind of power on this planet–green power, of course. Related: Trump, Endless Wars, and the Decline of American Empire Meanwhile, not just Donald Trump’s world but ours, too, now seems to be flailing, failing, and falling all at once, and that, believe me, is no small thing and would, once upon a time (in another imperial universe), have been literally inconceivable. And yet, here we are on a planet going down for all sorts of creatures , including us humans. Ni hao ma (or, translated from Chinese: How are you)? And the answer, in the age of Donald Trump, himself the personification of decline, and a rising China on a falling Earth is: Not so good, thank you.

articles.title: Healing the World Spirit
articles.author: Guest Author
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Inspired by Dr King’s call for “a spiritual revolution in values.” Diagnosis, Most of our societal challenges are the end result of a society whose values are void of spiritual considerations. We worship wealth and the wealthy which are outgrowths of prioritizing financial profit at the expense of life itself. We are totally unbalanced by injustice, making lies the order of the day. We regard dominators with awed respect which generates unimaginable cruelty. What is happening in Gaza is fatal spiritual sickness. It is terrorism inflicted on our citizens, who in the majority do not want their taxes funding atrocity and are traumatized by viewing it. The inability to be affected by this is also a trauma response. All of us are in dire need of healing. Gaza’s oppression is part of a strategy for crushing dissent, enlarging societal insanity guaranteeing widespread powerlessness and normalizing genocide, which is the plan for most of us. A new world of peace is possible with the implementation of a new valuation of spiritual health as necessary to our survival. The imbalance created by a value system that prizes the material or financial profit above all else is obvious. Our technological capacities so far outstrip our spiritual capacities that we are in danger of destroying all that is worth living for, if not our lives. The current meme "4 BILLION dead” is worth deeper consideration. We are on that ledge. It rivals any holocaust or disaster that human beings on this earth have ever experienced. This is where technological growth with no spiritual consciousness has landed us. Dr King’s call for “ a spiritual revolution in values” is our last best hope of surviving as a species with anything worth living for intact. Healing Modalities Uniting with new ways to live has become a global emergency. May we unite with the principles of Reverence for all that live, Balance in the form of justice so that all may live and prize Compassion primarily, overriding punitive and sadistic practices that presently dominate our lives and consciousness and threaten our survival. We use various tripartite forms to implement change because three is the number most aligned with change. Reverence, Balance & Compassion are capitalized here for clarity and emphasis. If we are to live, in the best sense of the word, we implement changes based on basic spiritual principles, capable of uniting people of all religions and ways of being. Peace is a result of living by these principles. Reverence is interwoven with love of life. Reverence which bears fruits of wonder, awe and humility are a part of every major religion on earth, however we should seriously consider going beyond the limitations of religious practices (while not banishing them because some are very useful), aligned as they are with institutions. Institutions are, by nature morally ambiguous and usually malevolent in their search for funding as their highest priority and often twisted too easily into harmful dogma. It is in the so called mystical traditions of major religions that spiritual wisdom may be found. Authentic spiritual growth may only be possible outside the strictures of most institutions, unless they are monasteries and even then it is limited. For spiritual growth to be widespread it must grow in the soil of all basic human rights, which are in dire need of update and expansion, being the rule rather than the exception. This would be a result of a value system that places spiritual health, in all of its infinite diversity, as a primary value. Liberty cannot exist without Balance in the form of justice. Balance is interwoven with justice. There can be no justice without truth. Living in truth is at the center of spiritual health. The definition of spiritual health must take into account the holistic nature of our existence. Balance is for us all. Poverty and oppression degrade not only the environment by the imbalance of the natural order, but also the human spirit. Compassion is the ability to see through the eyes of love, for everyone. This is a practice undergirded by spiritual health and spiritual practices which vary so widely because of their infinite variety that the freedom of possessing basic human rights, the definition of which must be expanded and treated as a building principle of the highest order, is essential. To enable the freedom to practice these modalities everywhere in all their infinite variety is the only guarantee of widespread human spiritual health. This is a fruit of Compassion implemented as a universal value. There can be no civil society without Compassion as a primary principle. Compassion is rooted in understanding holistic reality, or the interconnection of all life on this planet. The practice of Compassion generates understanding of the reality of wholistic unity. Unitive Consciousness One antidote is living in a world where wholistic visions are infinite and all decisions of import revolve around the core principle of “Do no harm” as primary directive. Is there a better directive? Wholistic vision is rooted in the practice of Compassion. We all wish for a deeper sense of Life. Liberty and the Pursuit of Happiness, none of which are possible without Reverence, Balance & Compassion as widespread universal practice & principles. The caveat is the replacement of “the pursuit of happiness” with a triumvirate of peace, contentment and bliss. Life is God. The life spirit is divinity. Liberty, or freedom, is not and never will be sustainable while most of us are oppressed by slavery. Happiness as an ideal is over rated, one might even say childish if not superficial. It is aligned with the selfishness that is killing us all. Peace and contentment are priceless antidotes to so much that ails us and are a practice of discipline rather than the giddy self delusion of chance when it indulges us, usually labelled as “happiness.". Reverence and awe are bliss when generated by the wonders of the life spirit. The book Ways of Being, Animals, Plants, Machines: the search for Planetary Intelligence , by James Bridle, illuminates the Unitive forms of intelligence utilized by many so called “lower forms”of life to live. There is a life spirit and many beings have far surpassed us in their abilities to live in alignment with it in ways we do not understand. Perhaps this understanding will require a new humility. The pursuit of happiness is an outmoded idea. The contentment, peace and bliss which, if we are fortunate, replaces the search for the more materially oriented “happiness", are spiritual in nature. The pursuit of happiness is aligned with craving which produces suffering. Planetary Peace is not possible without a widespread valuation of Compassion as a central principle of our culture(s). Yes, the world and life itself are by nature problematic with death, sickness and the unpredictability of nature expanded in our interiors because we fear this darkness and deny it thereby strengthening destructive power through fear. We can do so much better. This goal is an integral part of our largest task in life. The operative word here is “we.” It is the holding together of opposites that is the ultimate form of peacemaking. Black and white without grey are a game board cartoon all about war. Shades of grey are not only about dominator games but part of an educational process of understanding the infinite beauty, complexity and holistic integrity of life itself. Virginia Bryant Virginia Bryant is an award winning artist/painter currently working in upstate New York.

articles.title: A Brief Note on Marx: Capital as a Social Relation
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Douglas Dollinger Marx argues this case in his discussion of colonization (Chapter 33, Kapital, Volume 1). According to Marx, Wakefield, a prominent 19th-century writer on colonization, had discovered that capital is not just a thing but a social relation. Wakefield stumbles upon this revelation by accident. It is not a theme that features prominently in the political economy of Marx’s time or ours. It is, however, a central theme in Kapital and is pivotal to his notion of human emancipation. I want to explain what Marx means by this in simple terms. Students of Marx might find this note a bit too basic for Socialism 101, so maybe it is best to see it as a contribution to Socialism 100. Suppose you are a capitalist and that you show up with your capital – machines, factories, patents, etc. – in a land called Manuland. A bit about Manuland. In Manuland income earners work for themselves either in small manufactories or on small farms. A small manufactory is a one-person or several-person shop of some kind, a shoe shop, say. The people in the shop make the shoes, hence the “manufactory”. Let assume, too, that they own the means of production. We have here a small, self-sufficient college of cobblers. Suppose similar colleges of clothiers. Etc. Now assume the farmers in Manuland are one-family farms and that they own their own means of production. Let us finally assume that the cobblers and farmers are all getting by; sure, there are some bad years but, barring bad accident or ill health, they all get by. Both can afford to exchange a bit of their produce, should they enjoy a surplus, but neither can amass the surplus that drives capital accumulation. You show up now as a proud and ambitious capitalist in Manuland, but just before putting the shovel to the ground to build an industrial facility of scale, you discover something troubling: Manuland has no proletariat. Capital therefore has no place in Manuland. Why? Workers in Manuland do not have to depend on the capitalist for work; they have their own work and their own means of production. The political economy of capitalism, unlike the political economy of Manuland, necessitates a class of dependents; the dependency of this class moreover is a direct function of its having no ownership over the means of production. It is the limited privilege of ownership, and specifically ownership of the means of production, that separates the dependency class from the capitalist. Manuland has no capitalist conception of private property; capital as yet has no social significance in Manuland. In other words, capitalism cannot work if the laborerlabourer is free of capitalist dependency. The point deserving emphasis here is that capital itself is a social relation in the simple sense that it establishes a relation of dependency between those who own and those who do not. Those who do not own must work for those who do; given the reality of surplus value (Mehrwert) – workers create much more value than they get paid for – it is virtually guaranteed that their level of pay will not free them from the dependency. Nor of course is it designed to. On the contrary. Capitalism produces a proletariat of necessity; and dependency becomes a permanent feature of capitalist society. Most of us are aware of this dependency; we live it day by day; economists of a capitalistic bent, however, seldom mention it. If it registers at all in the thinking of these economists, it tends to be seen as simply rooted in the nature of human society itself. Capitalism requires that private property in the means of production be restricted to the few; workers by contrast are expected to sacrifice any claim to owning the means of production, an outcome that perpetuates the condition of dependency that constitutes and defines the proletariat. Understanding this notion of dependency opens the door to Marx’s conception of emancipation. Marx was of course keenly aware of the fundamental antagonism between capitalist dependency and the reality of human emancipation. How is it exactly that we can regard people as free who are in fact dependent for survival on a privileged few? Note, again, this few cannot become the many. A world of capitalists is a world without workers. Someone has to do the work, and it is best that this individual be compelled to do it; a free individual may opt not to do it. For capitalism to work, then, a large majority of people must be placed in a condition of dependency and kept there. Abe Lincoln called it wage slavery. Note here that unions can modify the conditions of such dependency and render them less onerous for workers, but they cannot eliminate the basic social relation of dependency that characterizes capitalism. This will require an organized political effort to overcome the exclusive privileges of ownership of private property in the means of production. Human emancipation in its fullest sense awaits the completion of this task. The post A Brief Note on Marx: Capital as a Social Relation first appeared on Rochester Red Star .

articles.title: Susan Collins’s Record: Making Injured Workers’ Lives Harder
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: Susan Collins has been the senator from Maine for twenty-nine years, during which time she’s received scrutiny for her coziness with corporate donors , her record on war with Iran , and her votes against lowering prescription drug prices, among other things. But one of the most impactful measures on Maine workers that she took happened well before she first went to Washington. In an episode that’s little remembered today, in the late 1980s and early ’90s, Collins led the way on a set of reforms to Maine’s workers’ compensation system that saw the state government shut down for the first time in its history and led to major cuts to injured workers’ benefits. Appointed to the task by an insurance-industry-friendly Republican governor, Collins — then a state official who had never held elected office — ardently pursued the changes, openly appealing to the insurance industry to help push them through, and pushing for far-reaching cuts that were only prevented because Republicans lacked the numbers in the state legislature. Collins has carved out a reputation as a moderate in the Senate, a reputation at odds with her tendency to vote in alignment with Donald Trump’s position more than 90 percent of the time. But as her early role in cutting benefits for injured Maine workers recalls, Collins has also had a long history as an ideologically driven servant of the business sector. “Absolutely No Heart” Though the workers’ comp reforms were the brainchild of, and set into motion by then-Governor John McKernan, Collins played a leading role. Reports at the time described her variously as “the administration’s point person on workers’ comp,” his “ top advisor ” on the issue, his “ key representative ” in legislative negotiations on the matter, and even the “ administration’s negotiator .” Collins herself saw it that way: when she ran for governor a few years later in 1994, she campaigned on the overhaul, taking credit for having “reformed workers’ compensation” and winning hard-fought “battles” to do so. One Democrat involved in the legislative talks, former state senator Gerard Conley Jr, later recalled her as “a very tough negotiator.” “She struck me as being extremely bright,” Conley said. “But I also felt she had absolutely no heart. She would get what she knew the governor needed at any cost — even if it included shutting down state government.” The reforms under Collins came in two waves. The 1987 round took rate-setting out of the hands of the legislature and put it in the hands of a single political appointee, leading to benefits being cut more than 40 percent and premiums being hiked more than 50 percent, with some of the most seriously injured workers bearing the brunt. The 1991 round cut benefits further for some workers and mandated that an independent medical examiner effectively judge in any dispute, streamlining the ability to deny worker claims. Those who pushed these cuts weren’t wrong that there were real problems facing Maine’s workers’ compensation system. By the late 1980s, the average cost for a permanent injury in the state was $67,861, nearly double that of the second-most expensive state. That and the threat of mass exodus in 1987 by fifteen insurance firms covering 75 percent of the market ostensibly triggered the push to make the overhaul. Yet for all these very real issues, critics charged that the cuts were driven more by ideology than data. One reason was that besides its most expensive workers’ comp costs, Maine also happened to have the country’s worst workplace safety record: 68 percent above the national average, on the eve of the second set of cuts in 1991. In fact, before the first set four years earlier, state officials, attorneys in workers disability cases, and members of the industry themselves had agreed this was a major reason for the skyrocketing costs. This fact would be largely ignored in the ensuing debate. Collins simply publicly insisted the real issue was “inflated benefits” while dismissing workplace safety concerns, saying that critics were simply charging “that Maine employers do not care about safety” and that she didn’t “think there is any evidence of that.” Yet after the reforms were a done deal, the governor’s own press secretary would admit that most of the money in the workers’ comp system didn’t actually go to injured workers. Then there was the fact that, for all of Collins’s claims that cutting workers’ comp would “retain and promote good jobs,” it was far from clear the two things were linked. In the run-up to the 1991 cuts, several experts questioned the claim they would create jobs; one called it “silliness,” while another called workers’ comp a “trivial cost” for businesses in the grand scheme that was only “ psychologically ” a burden for employers. By the Sun Journal’s calculation, the savings in the proposed cuts were enough to create jobs that would cover only a small fraction of Maine’s unemployed. Once the second set of cuts were signed into law, the Maine Sunday Telegram would report that “few companies that closed or laid off workers put the blame entirely on workers’ compensation.” In a Maine Chamber of Commerce and Industry survey conducted earlier that year of the seventy-five companies that took either measure, a mere two cited the cost of workers’ comp as the main reason, while only three others called it a contributing factor. There was also the administration’s ties to the insurance industry. Insurance superintendent Joe Edwards, who controversially approved the carriers’ exit from the Maine market, had previously worked in the insurance industry, and he would draw criticism for using words like “we” and “us” while trying to convince insurance executives to stay in the state. McKernan himself, the governor, had once lobbied for insurance companies. And Collins herself openly appealed to the industry, whose seal of approval for the reforms she sought . “We’re counting on the business community to mount a lobbying effort to push [McKernan’s cuts] through,” she told the Chamber of Commerce of the Greater Portland Region in October 1987. “It’s absolutely critical that you start today” to reach out to legislators, she urged them. Sure enough, business wound up spending nearly $50,000 on a lobbying effort for the 1987 reforms, and insurance executives and representatives turned up to the legislature on the day of the vote, reiterating their threats to leave to Democratic leaders. A few years later, insurance agents would receive a letter on behalf of the governor’s campaign calling him “a good friend to the insurance industry” and praising Collins and other appointees for their “knowledge of our industry and fair, balanced approaches to our problems.” This coziness with the industry helped feed accusations that the carriers’ threats to leave the state was a manufactured crisis , part of an “orchestrated” and “heavy-handed attempt to intimidate the legislature into giving them what they want,” as the Maine AFL-CIO charged . In any case, Collins would use the industry’s threats to build pressure for the cuts, repeatedly pointing to them to demand they be urgently pushed through, warning that Maine workers might imminently be left without coverage. Despite Collins’s assurances that the solution lay in simply giving the industry whatever it wanted — “to make a market [where] companies want to stay,” she said — the cuts didn’t seem to work. The industry continued to ask and get approval for sizable rate hikes in the years that followed despite the cuts, with the Democratic House Speaker complaining that “the only ones who seem to have profited from the [1987] ‘reforms’ are the insurance companies.” In Lockstep With Industry When 1991 rolled around, Collins was again in a leading role. Heading a task force to investigate whether it took too long for the clock to start ticking on workers’ benefits, she made clear her priorities were to cut costs, decrease litigation, reduce fraud, and get people back to work as quickly as possible. As nearly forty industry groups put together their own reform wish list, Collins admitted that her own package “parallels some of the themes advanced by” the employer coalition, and that there was “quite a bit of similarity ” to what they put forward. The task force would eventually recommend changes like giving employers more time to challenge claims, removing a penalty on employers who get workers at higher risk of reinjury back to work sooner, and having an independent medical examiner rule on workers’ disabilities. At a March meeting , employers complained to Collins that workers’ comp claims were driven by ambulance-chasing lawyers and complained it created a “subculture” of laziness. She was familiar with their concerns, she replied, and said it was too hard to cut workers off their benefits, which she claimed often went to non-work-related injuries. Elsewhere, she complained that too many claims were now “soft-tissue” injuries — a category that included carpal tunnel syndrome — rather than “the classic kind of industrial accident.” Collins advised the governor to veto a Democrat-passed package of workers’ comp reforms that would have made benefits more generous. She then embarked on a tour through the state to sell his package of cuts, with the administration’s own analysis found made two-thirds of its savings on the back of injured workers by, among other things, reducing eligibility. Already controversial, the reforms became the statewide issue in July after McKernan, to push them through over Democratic opposition, decided to link the package to the state budget, causing a more than two-week-long state government shutdown, the first in its 170-year history — a “ hostage ” situation, as one Democrat put it. At one point, the governor found himself barricaded inside his office as irate state workers stormed the state capitol in protest. With Democrats holding firm amid the furor over the shutdown, the administration was forced to compromise. The final version of the package was free of the eligibility restrictions and duration limits Collins had fought for but still kept some cuts and maintained the role of independent medical examiners, placing expansive unilateral power into the hands of a single individual to make or break an injured workers’ claim. Organized labor despaired . Collins told employers it was a “good signal” that should make them “take another look.” Yet this round of cuts didn’t work either. Meant to reduce the role and cost of lawyers, experts complained the overhaul did the opposite, adding litigation costs and making the system more complicated. The administration itself admitted cuts would only save enough to offset a 14 percent rate increase for employers, and pretty soon Collins was suggesting that more reforms were coming to keep trying to bring down costs. Less than half a year later, nine companies filed again to leave the Maine market and Collins once more was warning of a market collapse. The following January, the business lobby demanded more urgent cuts. Collins adamantly resisted one long-proposed solution to this: a state-run insurance fund that would inject competition into the industry and wouldn’t up and leave the market. Collins usually threw up objections based on the idea’s supposed impracticality: it would be too time-consuming or too expensive to set up, or that it wouldn’t reduce rates. But occasionally she made clear that she was against it on ideological grounds. That meant “advocating that the state government get into the workers’ compensation insurance business,” she wrote in August 1990, something she and the rest of the administration wouldn’t abide “because of our philosophical commitment to the private market.” “It is ironic that at a time when the rest of the world is moving away from state ownership and racing toward private enterprise,” she wrote, proponents of the idea want to “have the state operate an insurance company.” Moderate Sheen on an Anti-Worker Record Collins would not be part of the most far-reaching round of cuts that came in October 1992, having resigned that January to take a regional post in the Small Business Administration. But her efforts set the stage for those reforms, which would echo the more severe cuts her task force had urged. “This session of the legislature must do something” on workers’ comp, Collins said the day after filing her resignation. “There is a greater realization than ever before that workers’ comp is a great problem. When I came here [to Augusta] five years ago I had to convince people that it was a problem. I don’t have to do that now.” It took nearly thirty years for the Maine legislature to roll back the workers’ comp cuts that Collins backed and helped set into motion — an effort that, ironically, would be partially led by her current challenger for her Senate seat, Troy Jackson, in 2019. That year, Maine workers testified about the chaos and suffering that they had been plunged into after being injured on the job, thanks in part to a workers’ comp system plainly inadequate for making them whole, especially in the face of significantly higher living costs. If Collins survives another reelection campaign this November, it will be yet another Harry Houdini–like political escape for a politician adept at putting a moderate face on a record that has been devastating for US workers. articles.title: It’s Election Time Again
articles.author: W. D. Ehrhart
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. So here we are just days before the midterm election, and the anticipation is almost palpable. Last weekend, my wife and I went to a No Thrones No Crowns No Kings rally in our neighborhood, and the prevailing sentiment was clearly that a Big Blue Wave is about to sweep the Democrats into control of both the House and the Senate as well as making huge gains at the state level. I can’t help remembering that the prevailing sentiment in 2016 among Democratic voters and the political pundits was that Hillary Clinton was a shoo-in. How could she lose to a clownish buffoon who bragged about grabbing women by their genitals and claimed he could shoot someone on 5 th Avenue in broad daylight without consequences? But Democratic voters and the political pundits didn’t reckon on the ignorance, irrationality, venality, and bigotry of huge numbers of American voters. I’ve been told by at least one newspaper editor that I can’t say that; I’m not supposed to disparage my fellow citizens because I might insult them. All I can say to that is: so what? What are they gonna do? Vote for Trumpsters just to spite me? A significant portion of Americans don’t need me to encourage them to vote against their own self-interests, however backhanded my “encouragement” may be. Multiple elections since 2016 have demonstrated time and again that the MAGAMobster’s supporters don’t care about broken treaties or counterproductive tariffs, cuddling up to dictators or murdering civilians on the high seas, kidnapping foreign heads of state or waging unprovoked wars of choice, wrecking the White House while installing a gladiatorial arena on the lawn, ruining the Reflecting Pool while destroying the Kennedy Center, trashing our national parks and re-writing American history itself, gutting the environment or packing the Supremely Unjust Court with right-wing activist ideologues, surrounding himself with incompetent lackeys while engaging in blatant criminal corruption to the benefit of himself, his family, and his uber-rich friends. Related: All the News That’s Fit to Print? Whatever disillusionment may be developing among the MAGA ranks, as nearly as I can tell, seems to be based on the cost of gasoline and the price of eggs, not on the outrageously lunatic behavior of the grotesque parody of a president currently occupying what has become the Whitewash House. And that disillusionment is not likely to result in large numbers of MAGAMinions going out and voting for candidates like James Talarico, Sherrod Brown, Amy Klobuchar, or Abdul El-Sayed. After all, Trumpasaurus is not even on the ballot. And given MAGAVoters’ inability to understand that they’ve been getting screwed left and right not just by the current administration, but by the cowards in Congress who refuse to do their sworn duty to uphold and defend the Constitution, I have serious doubts about the outcome of the election that is about to take place. I have spent a lot of time in the past ten years trying to understand how so many people could be so thoroughly hoodwinked by this grifter and con artist, incapable of seeing what he really is or grasping the damage he is doing to their lives and the country we live in. And I think I have finally figured it out. The core of his support comes from white men. Yes, there are women who support Trump. The Daily Show’s Jordan Klepper repeatedly braved Trump rallies to interview, among the myriad white men, white women and even a few people of color. But it is white men who constitute the backbone of his support. And these men are convinced that, ever since the 1960s, women, people of color, homosexuals, and immigrants have stolen white men’s patrimony, white men’s right to privilege and domination, which they do not see as privilege and domination, but simply as what should be theirs by right. Related: Trying to Avoid Giving Up And these men are angry, furious, outraged. They believe all their problems and frustrations and disappointments and failures can be laid at the feet of these non-male, non-hetero, non-white upstarts. For the most part, they cannot say out loud what they think and feel and believe because it might have serious repercussions on their jobs and families and social relationships. But their president expresses the intolerance and bigotry and racism and hatred they feel, and he gets away with it. He glories in it. He basks in it. He speaks for them. He says what they cannot say. It doesn’t matter what he actually does. It doesn’t matter what his policies are or how they impact his supporters or what kind of damage they are doing to the nation and the world. Thoughtful people assume that voters are thoughtful people, but election after election in my lifetime, and long before my lifetime, has demonstrated that huge numbers of voters are not thoughtful or rational or capable of grasping the consequences of their vote. To say all this out loud is a kind of heresy, but history has proven me right time and time again. Related: The Sexual Picadilloes of Politicians So I just don’t have a whole lot of confidence that the voting public is going to behave any differently than it always has, and a lot of that voting public is going to act against its own self-interest and vote for candidates who either agree with their Felon-in-Chief or lack the courage to stand up to him. I hope I’m wrong. I hope all those folks who think a Big Blue Wave is coming turn out to be right. How could any sane person not hope for that result? But after a lifetime of disappointments—I am 78 years old—I find it all-but-impossible to place any faith in the majority of the American voting public doing the right thing on election day.

articles.title: Girl Child
articles.author: Elahe Amani
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. October 11, the International Day of the Girl Child, arrived amid a period of unprecedented turmoil and shifting political realities. From war and violence in Iran and Yemen to political unrest and violent protests across parts of Europe, including Albania and France, a climate of instability continues to threaten human rights, peace, and security. Across many parts of the world, the rise of religious extremism, authoritarian governance, and right-wing populist movements has intensified resistance to gender equality and undermined efforts to protect the rights, dignity, and safety of girls. Invoking tradition, religious authority, parental rights, and the preservation of the “natural family,” some of these movements seek to restrict women’s autonomy and weaken the institutions designed to protect women and girls. The recognition of the “girl child” as a distinct focus of international advocacy marked an important milestone in the global struggle for gender equality. At the Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing in 1995, The Girl Child was established as one of the 12 critical areas of concern in the Beijing Platform for Action. This recognition affirmed an essential principle: discrimination against women often begins in childhood, and addressing gender inequality requires specific attention to the rights, needs, and experiences of girls. The Beijing Platform addressed discrimination in education, health and nutrition, child labor, violence, harmful practices, and girls’ participation in social, economic, and political life. It helped institutionalize the girl child as a central category in international women’s rights advocacy, connecting the inequalities girls experience in childhood with the broader structures of gender discrimination that shape their lives. In subsequent years, UN General Assembly resolutions continued to address the rights of the girl child, while international agencies expanded their focus on girls’ education, child marriage, violence, exploitation, and adolescent health. In 2011, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 66/170, designating October 11 as the International Day of the Girl Child. The annual observance created an international platform to advance girls’ rights, amplify their voices, and recognize their leadership. Related: Iran’s Employment Crisis Is Driving Women Out of the Workforce The terminology itself also deserves reflection. The term “girl child” served an important political purpose: it made girls visible in policy discussions where the broader categories of “women” and “children” could obscure their distinct experiences of discrimination. Yet the history of this terminology is not without criticism. Historian Sarah Bellows-Blakely, in her work on the history of girl-focused development, examines how international development institutions have sometimes portrayed girls in the Global South primarily as vulnerable victims in need of intervention, rather than as individuals with agency, political voices, and diverse lived experiences. This critical perspective invites us to ask an important question: Who defines girls’ needs, whose knowledge shapes international policy, and how can girls themselves become active participants in decisions affecting their lives? Why does the girl child deserve our urgent attention today? Because recognition alone is not enough. The rights of girls remain threatened by the intersecting realities of poverty, armed conflict, forced displacement, disability, discrimination, and humanitarian crises. For girls living at the intersection of these vulnerabilities, the consequences can be especially severe. Consider the scale of the challenges facing children worldwide. More than 520 million children, over one in five globally, live within 50 kilometers of violent conflict events, according to research published by the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO). Approximately 1.6 billion children live in countries affected by conflict. These figures reflect different levels of exposure: proximity to violent events does not mean that every child experiences violence directly, but it highlights the enormous number of children growing up amid insecurity and instability. In conflict-affected communities, the destruction of schools ( the air strike on Feb 28, 2026 on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab 120 children killed ), loss of livelihoods, displacement, and breakdown of protective institutions can further heighten these risks. Discriminatory laws, harmful practices, and inadequate enforcement of children’s rights may allow these conditions to persist. Girls who are already marginalized because of poverty, ethnicity, disability, displacement, or other forms of discrimination may face multiple and overlapping barriers to protection. Related: Mother’s Day 2026: Reclaiming Motherhood as a Call for Peace, Justice, and Collective Care Poverty presents another profound challenge. According to UNICEF, approximately 412 million children lived in extreme monetary poverty in 2024, while an estimated 417 million children in low- and middle-income countries experienced severe deprivation in at least two essential areas of life, including education, health, nutrition, housing, sanitation, and water. These figures include both girls and boys and illustrate the magnitude of childhood deprivation, while underscoring the need for more comprehensive, gender-disaggregated data. Poverty, conflict, displacement, and discrimination do not operate in isolation. They intersect and reinforce one another, creating conditions that place girls at heightened risk of exploitation, violence, and child marriage. When families face economic hardship, armed conflict, or displacement, girls may be forced to leave school, lose access to health care and other essential services, or face decisions that prioritize immediate survival over their rights, well-being, and future. In some circumstances, child marriage is used as a misguided coping mechanism to reduce a family’s perceived financial burden, respond to insecurity, or conform to entrenched social and cultural expectations. The consequences of child marriage can extend throughout a girl’s life: interrupted education, early pregnancy, serious health risks, exposure to domestic and sexual violence, diminished economic opportunities, and restricted participation in decisions affecting her own future. The loss is not only individual. Families, communities, and societies are also deprived of girls’ talents, knowledge, creativity, and leadership. Child marriage, therefore, must not be understood simply as an isolated cultural practice or an individual family decision. It must also be examined within the broader social, economic, political, and institutional structures that constrain girls’ choices, perpetuate gender inequality, and undermine their fundamental rights. Globally, the legal landscape remains deeply concerning. According to UNESCO’s HerAtlas data, only 26% of countries set 18 as the minimum legal age of marriage without exceptions. In approximately 54% of countries, exceptions permit marriage before the age of 18, while in 18% of countries, laws still allow marriage below 18. These figures illustrate the gap between recognizing 18 as the appropriate minimum age and establishing an absolute legal prohibition on child marriage. The WORLD Policy Analysis Center’s legal database identifies numerous countries and jurisdictions where laws may permit girls to marry before the age of 18 under certain circumstances. These include Bahrain, Djibouti, the Federated States of Micronesia, Iran, Kuwait, Lebanon, Mali, Mauritania, North Korea, Pakistan, Qatar, Sudan, Timor-Leste, and Yemen. The United Kingdom also requires a jurisdiction-specific distinction: Scotland and Northern Ireland permit marriage at 16 under applicable legal conditions. The database additionally identifies Bangladesh, Botswana, Brunei, and the United Arab Emirates as having religious or customary law exceptions that may permit marriage below 18. These classifications should be checked against current national and subnational legislation, as laws and exceptions change over time. Particularly alarming is the evidence emerging from Iran, where technology is being used in ways that may facilitate and normalize child marriage. The Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) published an investigative report titled Child Marriage in the Digital Age , examining the Iranian government licensed matchmaking platform Adam va Hava (“Adam and Eve”) and its role in facilitating the marriage of minors. According to HRANA’s investigation, although the platform’s terms reportedly state that female users must be older than 15, its registration system accepts birth years corresponding to children as young as 12. Search filters reportedly allow users to browse prospective spouses from age 13, making profiles of minors accessible. These findings raise serious concerns about the protection of children online and the normalization of marriage involving girls who have not reached adulthood. The investigation also examines the platform’s institutional connections. HRANA traces its ownership to the Imam Reza Society, led by Hossein Yekta, a senior figure associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Yekta has been subject to European Union sanctions related to human rights violations. The platform has also reportedly received promotion through Iranian state media. HRANA situates its operation within a broader government-backed matchmaking system that expanded following the 2021 Youth Population Law, which encouraged the development of authorized matchmaking platforms. These developments must be considered alongside Iran’s Civil Code, which generally sets the minimum marriage age at 13 lunar years for girls and 15 lunar years for boys, while allowing marriage below those ages with the consent of a legal guardian and judicial approval. This framework falls far short of establishing 18 as an absolute minimum age for marriage and raises serious concerns about Iran’s compliance with international child-protection standards, including the principles of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The response from international civil society has been significant. HRANA and 23 other human rights organizations issued a joint appeal urging major technology companies to take action. They called on Google and Meta to remove the application from the Google Play Store and on Meta to address promotional accounts on Instagram and Threads. According to the appeal, an Instagram account with approximately 192,000 followers had been used to promote the platform and its matchmaking services, including content involving minors. The organizations also called for greater transparency regarding ownership, safeguarding measures, and the enforcement of child-protection policies. Related: Disconnected in War While after the joint appeal of HRANA and 23 other human rights organizations Google removed the "Adam and Eve" app from Google Play on October 9, 2026, for policy violations and Meta investigated the findings and removed related promotional and external entities from its platforms (including Instagram and Threads). However, this case raises a fundamental question: What responsibility do governments, technology companies, and international institutions have when digital platforms facilitate practices that place children’s rights and safety at risk? Technology should expand opportunities, access to information, and human connection, not provide new mechanisms for exposing children to exploitation or normalizing practices that compromise their autonomy and well-being. Child marriage is not simply a matter of tradition or private choice. When discriminatory laws permit it, institutions facilitate it, and digital platforms make it more visible and accessible, the issue becomes one of public accountability and the protection of fundamental human rights. Every girl has the right to childhood, education, bodily autonomy, safety, and the opportunity to determine her own future. Ensuring those rights requires unequivocal legal protections, effective enforcement, responsible technology governance, and sustained international action to eliminate marriage before the age of 18, without exceptions. The reality is that child marriage risks to girls' safety, physical integrity, health, and autonomy. In an extensive research on Child marriage and intimate partner violence: A global meta-analysis with the title of “ Prevalence of intimate partner violence among child marriage victims and the comparison with adult marriages: a systematic review and meta-analysis” 38 studies involving approximately 395,000 women married as children across five continents were reviewed and the findings are “ it is estimated that 35% had experienced intimate partner violence during their lifetime and 24% in the previous 12 months. Compared with women who married as adults, women married as children had 42% higher odds of experiencing intimate partner violence over their lifetime and 37% higher odds in the preceding year. Other research such as Honor-based violence against children: A systematic review with the title of “ Honor, violence, and children: A systematic scoping review of global evidence (2024) in the Journal Child Abuse & Neglect. This research identifies recurring harms including violence, family rejection and control, homicide, and forced or early marriage. The research highlights the risks of family violence and homicide, though it does not establish that child marriage itself causes honor killings. Child marriage in Iran and other countries where it is legally permitted requires a holistic examination of power dynamics, gender-based norms, and the ways violence is portrayed in the media and normalized in the public consciousness. The issue is not merely the occurrence of a crime, but also how such acts are represented sometimes in ways that normalize or even legitimize them. A crucial question is whether Iranian media is challenging these deeply rooted gender norms and defending women’s and girls’ fundamental rights to life, safety, and autonomy or, instead, reinforcing the very structures that undermine them. Combating so-called honor killings of the girl childs cannot be achieved simply by condemning perpetrators after the fact. It requires confronting the gender-based power structures that place girls in vulnerable situations, questioning the social and cultural norms that enable such violence, and ensuring that legal and institutional protections prevent child marriage and safeguard girls from harm. The legislative history of Iran’s Protection of Women Against Violence bill reflects the challenges of securing meaningful legal protection. Also referred to as the Protection, Dignity, and Security of Women Against Violence and later renamed the Prevention of Harassment and Promotion of Security for Women Against Misbehavior , the bill was reportedly withdrawn from the Islamic Consultative Assembly (Parliament) by President Masoud Pezeshkian’s cabinet in September 2025. For more than 15 years, the proposed legislation has moved back and forth among successive administrations, the judiciary, and Parliament, illustrating the prolonged struggle to establish comprehensive legal protections against violence toward women and girls. Related: March 8 in the Shadow of War: Iranian Women and the Enduring Struggle for Gender Justice Needless to say that child marriage is not only happening in global south. In the United States, as of October 8, 2026, 32 states reportedly still permit marriage before the age of 18 under certain legal conditions, including parental consent, court approval, or other exceptions. The laws vary significantly from state to state. California has recently prohibited marriage for anyone under 18, without exceptions, joining the states that have eliminated child marriage through legislation. The 32 states identified as still allowing marriage before age 18 are Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming. Nearly 300,000 children were married in the U.S. between 2000 and 2018. The vast majority were girls wed to adult men. Ending child marriage requires more than prohibiting marriage before the age of 18. It demands enforceable legal protections without exceptions, equal access to quality education, economic and social support for families, protection during humanitarian emergencies, and the meaningful participation of girls in decisions affecting their lives. On protecting the child girl rights, dignity and safety, we must move beyond celebrating girls’ potential and acknowledging their vulnerability. We must confront the structures that deny them safety, dignity, equality, and opportunity. Protecting girls means addressing not only the violations they experience, but also the intersecting inequalities and structural conditions that allow those violations to persist. Every girl deserves the freedom to grow up safely, complete her education, exercise autonomy over her life, and shape her own future. The promise of Beijing remains unfinished. Our responsibility is to turn its commitments into lived realities for every girl, especially those whose voices are too often unheard and whose rights are most at risk.
